en: Points of Controversy The Great Fifty The Twelfth Chapter
The Discourse on the Six Bases:
Is the eye-base a result of kamma? Yes.
Is it to be said that what is to be experienced as pleasant, what is to be experienced as painful, ... [and so on] ... has an object, and that there is for it turning back, ...
[and so on] ... aspiration? One should not say so. ...
Is it not the case that what is to be experienced as pleasant, ... [and so on] ... is without an object, and that there is for it no turning back, ... [and so on] ... no aspiration?
“Yes.
“If it is not to be experienced as pleasant … [and so on] … if it has no object, then there is for it no turning toward … [and so on] … no aspiration. Therefore, indeed, you should not say:
‘The eye-base is kamma-result. … [and so on] …
Is contact a result; is contact to be experienced as pleasant ...
[and so on] ... is it with an object; is there for it turning away ... [and so on] ... is there aspiration? Yes.
Is the eye-base a result (vipāka)? Is the eye-base to be experienced as pleasant? ... [and so on] ... has it an object? Is there for it turning toward [the object], ... [and so on] ... aspiration?

One should not say so. ... [and so on] ... Is the eye-base a result? Is the eye-base not to be experienced as pleasant? ... [and so on] ... has it no object? Is there for it no turning toward [the object], ... [and so on] ... no aspiration? One should not say so. ... [and so on] ...
“Yes.
“Then is contact a result; is contact not to be experienced as pleasant … [and so on] … is it without an object;
is there no turning toward it … [and so on] … nor aspiration for it?”
It should not be stated thus … [as before] … the ear-base … the nose-base … [and so on].
Is the tongue-base …pe… the body-base a result (vipāka)? Yes.
Is it to be said that what is to be experienced as pleasant …pe… has an object, and that there is for it turning toward [the object] …pe… aspiration?
One should not say so …pe… Is it not the case that what is to be experienced as pleasant …pe… is without an object, and that there is for it no turning toward [the object] …pe… no aspiration?
“Yes.
“If it is not to be experienced as pleasant … [and so on] … if it is without an object, then there is for it no turning toward … [and so on] … no aspiration. Therefore, indeed, you should not say:
‘The body-base is a result.’”
Is contact a result; is contact to be experienced as pleasant...
[and so on] ...is it with an object; is there for it turning away... [and so on] ...is there aspiration? Yes.

Is the body-base (kāyāyatana) a result of kamma (vipāka)? Is the body-base to be experienced as pleasant? ... [and so on] ... does it have an object (sārammaṇa)? Is there for it turning toward [the object], ... [and so on] ... and aspiration (paṇidhi)?

One should not say so. ... [and so on] ... Is the body-base a result of kamma? Is the body-base not to be experienced as pleasant? ... [and so on] ... does it lack an object (anārammaṇa)? Is there for it no turning toward [the object], ... [and so on] ... and no aspiration? One should not say so. ... [and so on] ...
“Yes.
“Is contact a result? Is contact not to be experienced as pleasant?
… [and so on] … is it without an object? Is there no turning toward it? … [and so on] … is there no aspiration for it?”
It should not be said so… [as before]… Should it not be said that “the six sense bases are karmic result”?
“Yes.
“Is it not the case that the six sense bases have arisen from the performance of kamma?
“Yes.”
If the six sense bases have arisen because of the performance of karma, then indeed, sir, you must say:
"The six sense bases are fruition.
The Discussion of the Six Sense Bases is finished.
